q: The BIA set an MTD of 12 h for the ordering system. The technical restore takes 8 h, and verification and entry of backlogged data (WRT) takes 5 h. What is the BEST conclusion?
options: The strategy does not meet the MTD because RTO + WRT is 13 h; a faster recovery strategy is needed.
The strategy is acceptable because the RTO of 8 h is less than the MTD.
The strategy is acceptable because WRT is not part of the MTD calculation.
The MTD should be increased to 13 h to align with technical capabilities.
explain: RTO + WRT ≤ MTD must hold. 8 + 5 = 13 h > 12 h. The MTD is a business decision from the BIA and is not adjusted to the technology; the strategy is adjusted.

q: Ransomware encrypted servers and deleted all backups on a domain-joined NAS, using a stolen administrator account. Which backup storage strategy would MOST LIKELY have prevented the loss of the backups?
options: Encrypting the backups with a strong algorithm.
An immutable (WORM / object lock) copy with separate credentials, outside the domain.
More frequent incremental backups to the same NAS.
RAID 6 on the NAS device.
explain: An immutable copy cannot be modified or deleted even with administrator rights until retention expires. Encryption protects confidentiality, not integrity/availability; RAID and more frequent backups to the same device do not help against deletion.

q: An organization does a full backup on Sunday and a differential backup every day. A failure occurs on Friday morning. What is needed for the restore?
options: Sunday's full and all differential backups from Monday to Thursday.
Only Thursday's differential backup.
Sunday's full and Thursday's differential backup.
Sunday's full and Monday's differential backup.
explain: A differential backup does not clear the archive bit, so it contains all changes since the last full. The last full and the last differential are sufficient.

q: A company has an MTD of three weeks for its internal training system and is looking for the most cost-effective recovery site. What should be recommended?
options: A hot site with synchronous replication.
A mirrored site in active-active mode.
A warm site with daily replication.
A cold site or a capacity agreement with a provider.
explain: With a long MTD, a cold site meets the requirement at the lowest cost. Hot and mirrored sites are a waste of money for a process that tolerates three weeks of disruption.

q: A company is designing the parking area and surroundings of its new headquarters and wants to reduce crime without visible "fortress" measures. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: CPTED: natural surveillance (visibility, lighting), natural access control (guiding movement) and territorial reinforcement
A 2.5 m fence with barbed wire around the entire complex
Armed guards at all entrances throughout the day
Removing all windows on the ground floor of the building
explain: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) uses the design of the environment (visibility, lighting, guiding movement, clear boundaries) to deter an attacker without an aggressive appearance. A high fence and armed guards are visible and more expensive measures, and removing windows endangers people's safety and does not address the outdoor area.

q: A flood destroyed the primary data center and systems are running from a hot site. The primary site has been restored. Which systems should be returned to the primary site FIRST?
options: The most critical systems, because they have the shortest MTD.
The least critical systems, to verify that the primary site works correctly.
All systems at the same time, to avoid a split environment.
The systems with the largest number of users.
explain: When returning, the least critical systems go back first; they serve as a test of the primary site, while critical systems stay at the alternate site until the primary has proven itself.

q: During a DR event, the company's e-mail system is unavailable and possibly compromised. How should the DR team communicate with employees?
options: Through team members' personal e-mail addresses, ad hoc.
Wait for the e-mail system to be restored.
Through predefined out-of-band channels (call tree, mass notification system, status page).
Through the company's public social media.
explain: The DR plan must define alternative, out-of-band communication methods in advance. A compromised channel is not used, and improvisation and public networks risk information leakage.

q: A storage array had 4 failures in a year (8,760 h), and the total repair time was 24 h. The RTO for that system is 4 h. What is the MOST accurate conclusion?
options: The MTBF is 6 h, so the system is unreliable.
The MTTR is 24 h, which is six times the RTO.
Availability is below 99%, so the SLA is not met.
The MTTR is 6 h, which exceeds the RTO of 4 h, so the recovery strategy does not meet the objective.
explain: MTTR = 24 / 4 = 6 h. The MTBF is about 2,184 h, availability about 99.7%. The key finding is that the average recovery time is greater than the RTO.

q: Who should give statements to the media during a major DR event?
options: Only the authorized spokesperson, with pre-approved messages.
The DR coordinator, because they have the best information.
Any manager the media contacts.
No one; the media is ignored until recovery is complete.
explain: The communications plan designates a single authorized spokesperson and approved messages. Ignoring the media leads to speculation, and multiple voices lead to contradictory information.

q: After a DR event, the team holds a meeting. What is the PRIMARY goal of the lessons learned activity?
options: To determine who is responsible for the delay and take disciplinary action.
To identify what needs improvement and update the DR plan and procedures.
To prepare a report for the insurance company.
To close the incident ticket.
explain: Lessons learned serves to improve the plan, not to find someone to blame. The result is an updated plan and an action plan with owners and deadlines.

q: An organization wants to confirm that the alternate site can really process production transactions, but without any risk to the primary systems. Which test is BEST?
options: Tabletop.
Full interruption.
Parallel test.
Read-through.
explain: A parallel test brings up systems at the alternate site and processes data in parallel while the primary runs normally. Full interruption endangers production, and tabletop and read-through do not prove the site works technically.

q: The DR plan has just been written and has never been tested. The IT manager proposes a full interruption test next week. What should be recommended?
options: Perform the full interruption because it is the only real proof.
Skip testing until the first incident occurs.
Perform the full interruption unannounced to make it realistic.
First perform less disruptive tests (read-through, tabletop, simulation, parallel), and a full interruption only with senior management approval.
explain: Tests progress gradually from the least disruptive. A full interruption carries the risk of an actual disaster and requires senior management approval and prior successful tests.

q: The team gathers in a conference room, a facilitator presents an earthquake scenario, and members discuss what each would do, without activating any systems. Which test is this?
options: Tabletop.
Simulation.
Parallel.
Checklist (read-through).
explain: A tabletop (structured walkthrough) is a group discussion through a scenario. A read-through is individual reading, and a simulation involves carrying out the response.

q: During a parallel test of the DR plan, what is MOST important regarding communications?
options: Communicate only with the IT team so as not to disrupt the business.
Clearly label all messages as a test and notify internal participants and relevant external parties (vendors, the DR provider, regulators if needed) in advance.
Test communications unannounced to get a realistic response.
Use the same channels as for a real disaster, without a test label.
explain: Messages during a test must be labeled as a test so they do not cause panic or real reactions, and external parties that are involved must be notified in advance.

q: A security manager is invited to participate in the annual BC exercise. What is the BEST way to ensure the exercise produces valuable results?
options: Focus the exercise exclusively on IT system recovery.
Do not define objectives so the exercise is spontaneous.
Define objectives and a realistic scenario based on the risk assessment in advance, involve business units and document findings in an after-action report.
Repeat the same scenario as last year for comparison.
explain: A BC exercise tests business continuity as a whole: objectives set in advance, a realistic scenario, business participation and a formal report that leads to a BCP update.

q: What is the MOST COMMON reason a BCP fails when an actual disruption occurs?
options: Overly detailed documentation.
The use of cloud services.
Too many participants in exercises.
The plan was not maintained or tested after changes in the organization.
explain: An outdated, untested plan is the main cause of failure. That is why the BCP lifecycle includes regular exercises and maintenance upon every significant change.

q: What is the role of senior management in BC planning and exercises?
options: It approves and supports the program, allocates resources and bears ultimate accountability.
It writes the technical recovery procedures.
It has no role until a disaster occurs.
It personally performs the full interruption test.
explain: Senior management provides the mandate, resources and approval and bears accountability (due care). Technical procedures are written by the teams.

q: How often should BC exercises be performed, according to good practice?
options: Only after an actual incident.
At least annually and upon every significant change to the business, sites or critical systems.
Every five years, with the BIA review.
Only when the regulator requires it.
explain: Good practice is to exercise at least annually and additionally upon significant changes, because otherwise the plan quickly drifts away from reality.

q: How should an electronic lock on the main exit of a building behave during a power outage?
options: Fail-secure, to protect assets.
Require a PIN on a battery-powered keypad.
Fail-safe (it unlocks), so that people can evacuate.
Remain in its last state.
explain: Human life comes first, so evacuation exits are fail-safe. Fail-secure is used for safes and the like, with a manual exit from inside.

q: A company is building a new data center and choosing a sprinkler system. What is the BEST choice?
options: Wet pipe, because it is the cheapest.
Deluge, because it quickly extinguishes large fires.
Dry pipe, because there is no water in the pipes.
Pre-action, because it requires two triggers and reduces the risk of false activation and leaks.
explain: A pre-action system fills the pipes only after detection, and a head opens only with heat, which makes it recommended for IT spaces. Deluge is for industry, dry pipe for cold spaces.

q: Employees report that unauthorized people are entering the building by following employees through badge-controlled doors. Which control solves the problem MOST EFFECTIVELY?
options: A mantrap (access control vestibule).
Additional CCTV cameras at the entrance.
A higher fence around the parking lot.
Locking the door for longer after passage.
explain: A mantrap lets one person through between two doors and directly prevents tailgating and piggybacking. CCTV only detects, and a fence does not affect entry into the building.

q: A bank employee is forced at gunpoint to open the vault. According to good practice, what is the CORRECT course of action?
options: Refuse and try to lock the vault.
Cooperate and discreetly activate the duress alarm or use a duress code.
Try to physically overpower the attacker.
Deliberately enter the wrong code until the vault locks out.
explain: Life is more important than assets; the employee cooperates and silently alerts security. Resistance and lockouts can provoke violence.

q: An engineer is traveling to a country with a high risk of industrial espionage and device inspection at the border. What is the BEST control?
options: Bring the usual laptop with full-disk encryption.
Leave the laptop in the hotel safe.
Use a loaner device with minimal data and reimage it on return.
Turn off Wi-Fi during the trip.
explain: A loaner device minimizes data exposure if it is seized or inspected and prevents a compromised device from being brought into the network. Encryption does not help if the password must be disclosed at the border.

q: An employee receives a series of unexpected MFA push requests at midnight. What should security training teach them to do?
options: Approve the request so the notifications stop.
Turn off the phone until morning.
Ignore the requests, because MFA protects the account.
Deny the requests and immediately report an incident to the security team, because the password is probably compromised.
explain: This is MFA fatigue (push bombing). The attacker already has the password; the user denies and reports so the password is changed and the incident investigated.

q: Order the DR plan tests from least to most disruptive to production.
options: Parallel test
Read-through (checklist)
Full interruption
Simulation
Tabletop / structured walkthrough
explain: A read-through is individual reading, a tabletop is a group discussion, a simulation carries out the response without failing over production, a parallel test does real processing at the alternate site while the primary runs, and a full interruption shuts down the primary site.

q: Match the description with the type of recovery site or agreement.
options: Space, power and HVAC without equipment; activation takes weeks.
Complete equipment and near-current data; activation in minutes to hours.
Some equipment and connectivity, data is not current; activation in hours to days.
Two organizations agree to host each other.
A provider guarantees reserved capacity in case of a disaster.
explain: A cold site has no equipment, a warm site has some, a hot site has everything and current data. A reciprocal agreement is a mutual arrangement, and a resource capacity agreement contractually guarantees capacity. A mirrored site (continuously active-active) is a distractor.
